slides.title: What a hallucination is
slides.summary: A hallucination is fluent, confident text that isn't true. It's the model doing what it was built to do, not a glitch in one place.
body: Ask a model for the author of an obscure paper and it may name someone, add a title and a year, all in a calm, authoritative tone. Every detail can be invented. That's a hallucination. Researchers also use the word confabulation: an arbitrary, incorrect answer that sounds right.

ul: Invented facts: a person, date or statistic that never existed.
Fake sources: citations, links, or function names in an API that don't exist.
Unfaithful summaries: a summary that contradicts, or adds to, the document you gave the model.
Faulty reasoning: steps that read fine but contain a wrong calculation or a leap of logic.

body: What they share is fluency. Fluent text is the thing a language model is best at, so how confident or polished an answer sounds tells you nothing about whether it's true.

body.note: A right answer and a wrong answer come out in the same tone. You can't judge accuracy from style.
It isn't limited to tricky questions. It happens on ordinary questions about things that are rarely written about, such as small companies, minor papers, and private details of people.

body: The next slides give four causes: what training rewards, what the data can teach, how models are graded, and how generation works. Then we look at how to detect and reduce it.

items.label: Invented fact
items.sub: “The 2019 paper Rapid Gradient Shaping was written by Dr. Alan Whitmore of MIT.”

viz.html: All four examples are invented for illustration. Each one would read as confident and well-formed.

slides.title: Cause 1: it predicts plausible text, not true text
slides.summary: Training rewards likely next words and never checks facts. The model also always has to output something.
body: Recall the training objective from the Training chapter: predict the next token of real text. A prediction is rewarded when it matches what the real text said, so the model gets very good at producing text that looks like real text. Truth only comes along for the ride, when real text happens to be true and consistent.

For a famous fact, the training text agrees with itself almost everywhere, so the model's probability piles onto one answer. For an obscure fact there's nothing consistent to learn, so the probability spreads over many names that all sound plausible. Compare the two cases on the right.

Generation then does the same thing in both cases: draw a token from the distribution and move on. A peaked distribution gives the right answer almost every time. A flat one gives an arbitrary answer, written in exactly the same confident voice.

body.note: The final softmax always returns probabilities that add up to 1. There is no "null" output. Saying "I don't know" has to be learned as ordinary text, and plain next-token training gives the model little reason to learn it.
Plausible and true line up when the training data is dense and consistent. They drift apart when it's thin or contradictory.

code: next_id = sample(probs)   # peaked: the right answer. flat: an arbitrary one

blocks.html: The distribution is peaked. Sampling gives the right answer nearly every time.
Prompt: “The author of the paper Rapid Gradient Shaping is Dr. ___” (no such paper exists)
The distribution is flat. Every name sounds fine, and whichever is drawn is stated as confidently as “Paris” would be. Numbers are invented for illustration.

slides.title: Cause 2: facts seen once can’t be learned reliably
slides.summary: A model learns patterns from many examples. An arbitrary fact it saw once, or never, gives it nothing to generalise from.
body: Some knowledge has structure the model can learn: spelling, grammar, how code is laid out. Millions of examples teach the pattern, and new cases follow it.

Other knowledge is arbitrary: a person's birthday, the author of a paper, a phone number. No pattern predicts it. The model can only get it right if it saw that exact fact, and saw it often enough to store it.

Count how many facts appear exactly once in the training data. Call that share the singleton rate. A 2025 OpenAI paper (Kalai et al., Why Language Models Hallucinate) argues that for arbitrary facts, a pretrained model's error rate has a floor of about that share. If 20% of birthdays appear exactly once, expect it to get at least roughly 20% of birthday questions wrong.
The intuition: a single sighting isn't enough to tell a true fact from a plausible alternative. Drag the slider to see how the floor moves.

body.note: It's a floor for facts with no learnable pattern, in a model that has only been pretrained (the paper's setting). More data and bigger models shrink the singleton rate, but real text always has a long tail of rare facts.
Hallucinating on rare facts doesn't mean the model is badly trained. It's a statistical consequence of learning from finite text.

slides.title: Cause 3: tests reward guessing
slides.summary: Models are tuned and graded on tests where a guess can earn points and “I don't know” earns nothing, so guessing becomes the winning habit.
body: Pretraining explains why hallucinations start. Why do they survive the later training stages? The same OpenAI paper points at how models are scored.

Most benchmarks grade like an exam with no negative marking: a right answer scores 1, a wrong answer scores 0, and "I don't know" also scores 0. Under that rule a guess is never worse than abstaining, so a model tuned to score well learns to always answer, however unsure it is. In the paper's words, models are optimised to be good test-takers.

Say the model is right with probability p when it guesses, and a wrong answer costs a penalty k (zero in most benchmarks). Guessing scores p − (1 − p)·k. Abstaining scores 0. So guessing only wins when p > k / (1 + k). With k = 0 that threshold is 0, so guessing wins at every confidence level.

The paper's proposed fix isn't a new hallucination test. It's to change how the existing, widely used benchmarks score answers, so a confident error costs more than saying "I don't know". For example: answer only if you're at least 75% sure, and a wrong answer costs 3 points. Try the three grading rules on the right.

body.note: Hallucination isn't only about what the model knows. It's also an incentive problem in how models are trained and graded.

code: def expected_score(p, penalty):   # p = chance the guess is right
return guess, abstain          # guess wins when p > penalty / (1 + penalty)

slides.title: Cause 4: one wrong token leads to more
slides.summary: Text is generated one token at a time with no backspace, so an early mistake becomes context the model then tries to stay consistent with.
body: Generation is a loop (see The big picture): each token is added to the context and the model continues from there. There's no step where it goes back and deletes a sentence. Once a wrong claim is in the text, it becomes evidence for what comes next.

Researchers call this hallucination snowballing (Zhang et al., 2023). They asked models questions where the first answer tended to be wrong, then watched them justify it with further false claims. When the same models were asked about those false claims separately, they could often see the errors: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2-70B-chat identified 67%, 87% and 94% of them. The effect persisted with higher temperature, beam search and zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting.

body.h: Other things that add to it

ul: Sampling: at a high temperature or loose top-p, a low-probability token is more likely to be drawn, and one odd token can send a sentence somewhere untrue (see Output & inference).
Long contexts: details buried in the middle of a very long prompt are recalled less reliably, so the model fills gaps with plausible guesses.
Stale knowledge: after its training cutoff the model doesn't know what has changed, yet it still answers in the present tense.

body.note: Verify claims in a fresh call. A separate prompt asking "is this statement true?" isn't tied to the earlier text, which is why the models in the study could catch many errors they had just made.

steps.caption: There is no such paper. The title is invented for this example.

item.label: It was written by Dr. Alan Whitmore at MIT.

The question now assumes Whitmore is real. The model's own earlier sentence counts as evidence.

item.label: Whitmore also wrote “Adaptive Momentum Schedules” (2021) and co-founded a startup.

steps.caption: To stay consistent with its earlier reply, the model invents more. The error compounds.

item.label: (New chat) Is there really a paper called “Rapid Gradient Shaping”?

steps.caption: Asked on its own, a model is far more likely to say it can't find one. In the study, models spotted most of their own false claims when asked separately.

slides.title: Inside the model: a “don’t know” default that misfires
slides.summary: Anthropic found a built-in “I can't answer” default that a feeling of familiarity switches off. When the familiarity is wrong, the model makes something up.
body: Interpretability researchers at Anthropic traced what happens inside Claude 3.5 Haiku when it's asked about people (Lindsey et al., 2025). Their finding cuts against the intuition that a model answers by default and sometimes stops itself:

ul: The default is to decline. A circuit that is on by default makes the model say it doesn't have enough information to answer.
Familiarity switches it off. When the model recognises the subject (the example is Michael Jordan), "known entity" features suppress that default and the model answers.
An unfamiliar name stays declined. For an invented name like Michael Batkin, nothing overrides the default, so the model says it doesn't know.

body: A misfire happens when the model recognises a name but knows nothing else about the person. The "known entity" feature fires anyway, switches off the "I don't know" default, and the model now has to produce an answer, so it produces a plausible but untrue one. In an experiment, the team made the model hallucinate on purpose by artificially boosting those known-answer features.

body.note: The model isn't being reckless. A recognition signal overrides a "don't know" default that was otherwise working.

This is one mechanism, in one model, on the topic of people. Other hallucinations will have other causes and other models may differ. What it shows is that recognising a topic and actually knowing the answer are separate signals, and they can disagree.

A name the model has seen, but knows nothing else about

slides.title: Detecting hallucinations: ask several times
slides.summary: If a model really knows the answer it gives the same answer every time. If it's guessing, the answers scatter.
body: A model's confidence in a single answer is hard to read, because fluent text hides it. But you can ask the same question several times and compare the answers.

Semantic entropy (Farquhar et al., Nature, 2024) does exactly that. Sample several answers, group the ones that mean the same thing, and measure how spread out the groups are. Answers that agree in meaning give a low value (the model probably knows). Answers that scatter give a high value (it's probably confabulating).
Grouping by meaning matters: "Paris" and "It's Paris." are the same answer even though the words differ. In the paper a second language model judges whether two answers mean the same.

The method needs no labelled examples of hallucinations, and in the paper's tests it beat simpler measures. The cost is several samples per question plus the judging step, so it's used where reliability is worth the extra compute.

ul: Verification outside the model: run the code, look up the citation, check the number in a database.
A separate fact-check call: ask a fresh prompt whether a claim is true, as in the snowballing study.
A second model as reviewer: have another model flag claims that lack support in the provided sources.

code: groups = cluster_by_meaning(answers)   # a second model judges 'same meaning?'
p = [len(g) / len(answers) for g in groups]
entropy = -sum(x * log(x) for x in p)  # high means the model is guessing

blocks.html: Question: “What is the capital of France?” Five samples:
All five answers mean the same thing. The model is consistent, so the answer is more likely to be reliable.
Question: “When was Dr. Alan Whitmore born?” (a made-up person) Five samples:
Every answer differs. The model has nothing to retrieve, so the scatter gives it away even though each single answer would have sounded confident.

slides.title: Reducing hallucinations: where each defence sits
slides.summary: Hallucination can't be removed at the source, so assistants lower its chances, check outputs, and let the model say “I don't know”.
body: The causes are statistical and about incentives, so no single fix removes hallucination. Real systems stack defences, and most of them are layers you've already met in Assistant architecture:

ul: Give the model the facts. Search and retrieval (RAG) put real source text in the context, which turns recall from memory into reading. The model can still misread a source, which is why good answers cite specific passages.
Make “I don't know” a good answer. Reward calibrated abstention in post-training, grade with scoring that penalises confident errors, and tell the model it's fine to say when it's unsure.
Use tools for exact things. A calculator for arithmetic, a code runner for code, a database lookup for records.
Check the output. Consistency checks like semantic entropy, citation verification, or a second model reviewing claims.
Design the product honestly. Show sources, mark uncertainty, and keep a person in the loop for high-stakes use such as medical, legal and financial answers.

body.note: If you're building an app: ground answers in your own data, require citations, and test with questions whose answers you know, including ones the model should refuse. Measure the hallucination rate on your own data, not just on public benchmarks.
Grounding reduces hallucination but doesn't eliminate it. Models can still misquote or over-generalise a source. Treat a citation as a way to check an answer, not as proof it's right.

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.summary: You've seen the model and the system around it. Building both yourself is the best way to make it stick.
body: You've now seen every component in a modern decoder-only LLM, and the system that turns it into an assistant. The best way to lock it in as an engineer is to build both.

ul: Andrej Karpathy, "Let's build GPT" and nanoGPT: a GPT in a few hundred lines of PyTorch.
"Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017): the original paper, readable after this course.
Jay Alammar, "The Illustrated Transformer": more diagrams of the same ideas.
Anthropic's constitution and system prompt release notes, and OpenAI's Model Spec: how labs write down intended behaviour.
"The Instruction Hierarchy" (Wallace et al., 2024) and "Defeating Prompt Injections by Design" (CaMeL, 2025).
The MCP specification and Simon Willison's writing on prompt injection.
"Why Language Models Hallucinate" (Kalai et al., OpenAI, 2025) and "How Language Model Hallucinations Can Snowball" (Zhang et al., 2023).
Anthropic, "Tracing the thoughts of a large language model" (2025) and "Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy" (Farquhar et al., Nature, 2024).

body: Three good exercises: implement the 4-token attention from the Attention chapter in plain Java or TypeScript and check your numbers match. Then write the 15-line tool loop from Assistant architecture against a real API, and add a permission check before each call. Finally, pick one question you know the answer to and one about an obscure person. Ask each one five times at temperature 1 and compare how much the answers vary.
